name: Adenosine
high_alert_note: ISMP's 2024 acute-care high-alert list includes intravenous antiarrhythmics; adenosine is an IV antiarrhythmic. summary: Intravenous antiarrhythmic used to convert paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia to sinus rhythm. Nursing focus: heart block and asystole, resuscitative readiness and the very short action of the drug.
evidence_type_note: The evidence here is a regulator product label (prescribing information written for prescribers and pharmacists). It is not a bedside nursing practice guideline: the nursing actions are inferences from label warnings, marked partial, and the unit's protocol governs practice.
jurisdiction_note: US FDA label only. EMA, MHRA and SFDA labels were not read; indications, warnings and presentations differ by country and by manufacturer.

items.text: The label indicates intravenous adenosine for conversion to sinus rhythm of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, including that associated with accessory bypass tracts, when appropriate vagal manoeuvres have not been effective.
Appropriate resuscitative measures should be available when the drug is given.
Continuous ECG monitoring and recording during administration follow the unit's protocol.

The label calls for caution and watching for respiratory compromise in patients with obstructive lung disease, since bronchoconstriction has been reported, and advises caution if the patient is also receiving digoxin, or digoxin with verapamil together, because of reports of ventricular fibrillation in that setting.

The registered rapid-bolus product label advises avoiding adenosine in patients with bronchospasm or bronchoconstriction, including asthma, and exercising caution with non-bronchoconstrictive obstructive lung disease. Severe respiratory difficulty requires stopping further administration and urgent assessment.

The registered label reports seizures and loss of consciousness after administration and describes interactions that may alter response or conduction. Review concurrent medicines before use and seek urgent clinical assessment for new neurological findings.
Adenosine decreases conduction through the AV node and may produce short-lasting first-, second- or third-degree heart block.
Patients who develop high-level block on one dose should not be given additional doses (a prescriber decision).
Transient or prolonged episodes of asystole have been reported, some fatal, and ventricular fibrillation has rarely been reported.
Because of the very short half-life, effects are generally self-limiting.

The registered rapid-bolus product is contraindicated in second- or third-degree AV block or sinus node dysfunction (unless a functioning artificial pacemaker is present), and with known adenosine hypersensitivity. Clarify rhythm and relevant history with the treating clinician before administration; the product does not convert atrial fibrillation, flutter or ventricular tachycardia to sinus rhythm.
Facial flushing was the most frequently reported reaction in the controlled trials the label summarises, with headache and sweating also reported.

Call for emergency help for severe respiratory difficulty, prolonged asystole, high-grade heart block or a dangerous rhythm with clinical deterioration. Do not give further adenosine after a serious reaction without clinician reassessment. Activate emergency assessment for seizure, unexpected loss of consciousness or significant circulatory compromise; do not give further treatment without reassessment.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record the rhythm strip, the response and any adverse event per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Keep resuscitation equipment and trained staff immediately available.
Watch the ECG continuously for heart block or asystole.
Note flushing, headache or chest discomfort.
Call for help immediately for prolonged asystole or a dangerous rhythm.
Screen for asthma, bronchospasm and obstructive lung disease before administration; clarify suitability with the treating clinician and watch breathing alongside continuous ECG.

Review current medicines with the team for altered adenosine response, including dipyridamole, methylxanthines and carbamazepine. Report loss of consciousness, seizure or unexpected conduction disturbance immediately.
Record the rhythm strip and response.
Verify the assessed rhythm, history of conduction disease, pacemaker status and allergy with the treating team before administration.
